meta.wording_rule: Better: the 95 % interval of the T1 difference excludes zero, the winner's median answer tokens are no higher, and the sign agrees on at least three of T1, T2, T3 and the questions (floors: T1, T2, T3). arms.name: Relational store (SQLite)
arms.what: The extracted facts (typed nodes such as files, functions, routes, tables and settings, and typed edges such as imports, calls, HTTP route to client call, test to code, table reads and writes, and co-change history) loaded into SQLite tables with indexes in both directions.
arms.reads: Only the facts built from the parent commit of each task (never the task commit or anything later).
arms.answers: A recursive SQL query walks from the seed file and symbol over the typed edges, scores every reached file, and the shared packer prints the best files first as a path line plus the signature lines of their definitions until the token budget is used.

arms.name: Graph engine LadybugDB
arms.what: The same facts loaded into LadybugDB, an embedded property-graph database with typed variable-length paths and a graph-algorithm extension (PageRank, Louvain communities, k-core).
arms.reads: The same fact files as the relational store.
arms.answers: Native graph queries for the walk; the same ranking and packer. Its best native form (S2) adds a stored Louvain community grouping to personalised PageRank; the PageRank iterations themselves run in application code.

arms.name: Graph engine DuckDB with DuckPGQ
arms.what: The same facts in DuckDB with the DuckPGQ extension, which adds property-graph queries (bounded variable-length paths, PageRank) to SQL.
arms.reads: The same fact files as the relational store.
arms.answers: Property-graph and recursive SQL queries for the walk; the same ranking and packer. Its k-hop walk is recursive SQL, not a graph operator.

arms.name: Reference implementation (plain in-memory code)
arms.what: A plain JavaScript implementation of the shared specification, holding the graph in memory.
arms.answers: Computes the same walk and ranking directly. Used only to check that the three stores return the same answers; never scored.

arms.name: Scripted text search
arms.what: A fixed script modelled on the searches sessions run: text search of the source tree for the seed's names, its module path and its route strings, then follows the seed's import lines. It is a fixed script, not an agent searching with judgement.
arms.reads: The source tree exported at the parent commit, plus (for its padding tail) the earlier commit history.
arms.answers: Ranks files by weighted hit counts, then appends a co-change padding tail (files that changed together with the seed file in earlier commits); same packer and budget as every arm.

arms.name: Same-directory floor
arms.what: No search and no graph: the files in the seed's own directory, then its capability folder, then outward.
arms.reads: File paths at the parent commit.
arms.answers: Prints those files in that order with their signature lines until the budget is used. Every method must beat it.

arms.name: Co-change floor
arms.what: No search and no graph: the files that changed together with the seed file in earlier commits, most often and most recently first, then the same-directory order.
arms.reads: Earlier commit history (ancestor commits only, same-PR siblings dropped) and file paths.
arms.answers: Prints those files in that order with their signature lines until the budget is used. Every method must beat it.

frozen_configurations.arm: relational, LadybugDB and DuckPGQ (the same configuration in all three)
frozen_configurations.plain: Walk from the seed over every base edge class (structure, imports, calls, HTTP, tests, data, settings and co-change history) in both directions with no hop limit, using edges of confidence 0.5 or more; rank reached files by degree-normalised spreading (each node passes its score on, divided by its number of edges); show files with their signature lines; no padding tail.

frozen_configurations.role: S1 (the choice of the tie rule as first written)
frozen_configurations.plain: The same walk limited to 4 hops, ranked by personalised PageRank (restart 0.30, co-change weight 1). The rule as first written picked it because "hops=4" sorted first by name among 15 tied configurations.
Unbounded walk; personalised PageRank fused with the stored Louvain community grouping of the engine as a locality prior. Scored on the stored grouping and on four further community draws.
One round of text search for the seed's names and module path (route strings off), seed imports followed, then the co-change padding tail.
One round with route strings on, co-change ranking fused into the search ranking by reciprocal rank fusion, then the co-change padding tail.
File granularity, signature form, same-directory order.
File granularity, signature form, co-change order then same-directory order.

sets.sentence: Given one changed file and symbol of a real commit as the seed, find the other files and definitions that the same commit changed.

sets.name: Cross-runtime subset of T1
sets.sentence: The T1 tasks from commits that changed more than one runtime (mobile app, backend, web); descriptive only because there are few commits.

sets.name: Tests to update

sets.name: Documented chains
sets.sentence: Chains of connected files written down in the project's own documents (the lifecycle audit, the open-work handoff and the invariants in CLAUDE.md): seed = the first named file, reference = the others, with the document removed from the facts.

ranked_hash_differences.explanation: The 8 (arm, task) pairs are 2 distinct queries: one seed at one parent commit appears in T1, T1x and T2, and another in T1 and T2. In every pair the shown items (80 or 86 items, scores included), the budgets, the seeds and the 50-path sample beyond the budget are identical, and every score field is identical. timeline.what: What is varied (facts, algorithm, output, engine), the task sets, the arms, the scoring and the statistics were written down. Held-out tasks (75 commits from July and August) were set aside to be run once.
Every arm moved into one Linux image after LadybugDB's algorithm extension would not load on Windows; running the graph side without it would have handicapped it.
timeline.caught: A handicap to one arm on Windows.
timeline.changed: One Linux image for all arms; facts still built on Windows from the same files.

timeline.what: One shared extractor built typed nodes and edges at each task's parent commit, cached by commit; both stores load the same files.
Audits of scoring, facts and the search arm before any configuration was chosen.
timeline.caught: The old scoring rule credited a bare list of every code file with 0.94 recall, so it could not tell arms apart; the search arm had selected its own configuration on its own labels; extractor gaps (mobile config reads, SQL in strings, URLs in loops and ternaries, Protocol-typed calls); a co-change rule beyond the protocol.
timeline.changed: Content scoring (a definition counts only when its own lines are shown); one scorer run only by the grader; padding made a shared option every arm may use; search labels sealed and its self-selection voided; extractor fixed and every arm re-run.

timeline.when: 2026-11-12 evening, before any arm was scored
timeline.what: Audits of the arms against the shared specification.
timeline.caught: Two arms divided by zero and two dropped a term in degree-normalised ranking at nodes with no out-edges; weighted shortest path defined differently in the two graph engines; LadybugDB communities differed with each store build; DuckPGQ computed path lengths beyond the hop limit.
timeline.changed: One definition for each; communities stored once per graph and reused; DuckPGQ fixed; equal stage-2 budgets (20 configurations per arm) and a parsimony rule; held-out comparisons H1 to H5 declared in advance.

timeline.what: 60 configurations for each of relational, LadybugDB, DuckPGQ and search (40 one factor at a time, then 20 proposed from each arm's own table), 8 for each floor, all on the 65 tuning commits.

timeline.caught: The tie measure (median tokens) was inert because every answer fills its budget, so the choice fell to alphabetical order and picked "hops=4", the weakest of 15 tied configurations.
timeline.changed: Ties broken by higher tuning primary instead; the first choice kept as row S1 and run on held-out so the change can be checked; harness records keyed by arm and configuration.

timeline.what: Checks of the run plan, the lock and the question code before the held-out run.

not_shown_by_this_test_addendum6_section: 19. Whether an agent finishes a task faster or with fewer mistakes with any of these tools. No agent was run.
20. Context that a change needed but did not edit. The reference is what the commit changed.

must_not_claim_claims_refuter: The graph engine does not help / graph models add nothing (H1 and H2 are identical by construction; H1b tested one native mode on one repository).
The three engines are equally fast, equally cheap or equally easy to use (H5 has not been reported; H1 and H2 concern answer quality only).
LadybugDB's native algorithms are proven equivalent to relational on every task set (T2 -0.037 [-0.084, 0.007] is not inside plus or minus 0.05, and community draw 1 gives 'inconclusive').
A typed code graph beats search across the codebase (the T1 win comes from mobile-seeded changes; on backend and web seeds it cannot be told apart from zero).
The typed store beats co-change history (the typed configuration itself contains co-change edges, and outside mobile seeds it ties the co-change floor at +0.001 [-0.051, 0.055]).
The typed store beats how sessions search today (the search arm is a scripted search whose recall is half co-change padding and which does not beat the co-change floor).
The typed store gives at least 0.05 more recall than search or the floors (the lower bounds are 0.036 and 0.019).
The typed store answers code questions better than search (H4 is inconclusive).
The typed store answers questions with 20 times fewer tokens (the two arms count tokens differently; final answers are about the same size).
Typed answers cost no more tokens than search (every answer fills its 8,000-token budget, so the tokens condition never decided anything).
The graph helps most on cross-runtime changes (on T1x every arm scores 0.49 to 0.54, and floor-dir and search s2 score at or above the typed stores).
An agent finishes tasks faster, or makes fewer mistakes, with the typed store (no agent was run).
The result holds for other repositories, or for context that is needed but not changed (one repository; the reference answers are files and definitions changed in the same commit).
The T3 interval shows a large effect on documented chains (25 tasks from 4 parent commits and 3 documents, clustered per task).
The amended selection rule picked the better configuration (s1 scored +0.011 [-0.004, 0.026] higher on held-out).
must_not_claim_discipline_refuter: That 23 held-out questions had untouched handling in every arm: search's question 25 target changed during pre-flight, so the subset for H4 against search is 22.

That no held-out question answer was known or examined before the run: auditors computed the expected typed-arm answers to setting questions 25, 33, 41 and 47 from the facts, and the question-47 result drove a code fix (no reference answer was used).

That the three typed arms returned byte-identical answers to the reference arm on every held-out task: shown content is identical on 770 of 770, but the full ranked-list hash differs on 5 (relational) and 3 (DuckPGQ) primary tasks.
That the question-40 cut-back gave the typed arms an answer: all three still answer [] (empty).

That arm processes could see no sealed material at all: /repo exposes untracked copies of the sealed NOTES and stats files (no held-out answers or ids) and the full git history. Hiding later commits rests on the arm code (git archive at the parent), not on the mounts.
That any held-out run was repeated or superseded: there were 0 repeats and 0 superseded files.
That the plan's global order of n was followed: only the order within each arm was.
further: Median answer tokens are 7,999 for every arm and set, so the 'no higher tokens' condition of the wording rule was always a tie and never decided a verdict.

T3 references carry no commit field, so score.js clusters T3 by task (25 clusters) although they come from 4 parent commits and 3 documents; T3 intervals are probably too narrow. 20 of the 25 T3 removals were no-ops by design (the document did not yet exist at the parent).
T1x (9 commits) and T4 (8 tasks, 4 fix commits) are descriptive only; their intervals are very wide.

H4 applies the item-18 wording to macro F1 over questions (interval of the F1 difference, median tokens per question, sign over T1, T2, T3 and questions); the H3 question signal uses the all-30 F1 difference with judgement items.

The share of reference definitions with no node uses my own matching rule (symbol node of the same path starting on the definition's first line, or same last name containing that line): held-out T1 354 of 3,150 (11.2 %), variables and objects 252 (8.0 %); the same rule on TUNE gives 212 variables and objects (5.1 %) where the audit reported 182 (4.4 %) by its method, so the two counts are not strictly comparable.
Runtime split is by the seed file's top folder (backend/, src/ = web, technician-app/ = mobile); web has only 7 commits.
The held-out judgement items (7) were taken from sealed/tq_agreement.txt; all 7 are items both readers left out, so removing them only removes answer items.

examples.rule: From the 388 TUNE T1 tasks whose reference has 3 to 8 units (files plus definitions), so that an example fits on the page: (1) typed clearly beats search = typed recall minus search recall at 8,000 tokens of at least 0.30; (2) tie = typed, search and the co-change floor all have the same recall, strictly between 0 and 1; (3) search or the co-change floor beats typed = the better of the two minus typed of at least 0.30. In each group the tasks are sorted by that difference (for the tie, by reference size), then by task id, and the median task is taken (the lower one when the count is even). Never held-out.

labels_corrected.statement: DuckPGQ's k-hop is recursive SQL, not a graph operator (bounded hops: a recursive SQL statement; unbounded: iterativelength() over a CSR built in the statement).
qualification: The first clause ("recursive SQL, not a graph operator") is true for the bounded classes S1 and base only. For the frozen primary (unbounded) DuckPGQ reaches nodes with iterativelength(), a graph function of the extension over a CSR, and fetches the reach DAG with a GRAPH_TABLE MATCH one-edge pattern (arms/duckpgq/pgq.js khop). The parenthesis says so; the headline clause should not be quoted alone.

labels_corrected.statement: LadybugDB's personalised PageRank runs in application code over a cached adjacency (40 iterations in JavaScript over a transition CSR fetched by one Cypher query and cached per configuration).
SQLite's walk is a recursive common table expression (bounded hops; unbounded hops use a level-wise loop of SQL statements driven by application code).

Where the frozen primary's ranking (degree-normalised spreading, addendum 2 item 20) runs: LadybugDB fetches arcs and out-degrees by Cypher and spreads the activation in application code (JavaScript), so for LadybugDB this ranking is not in the engine; SQLite and DuckPGQ spread it in SQL, one statement per BFS level, the level loop driven by application code; SQLite's unbounded walk is likewise a level loop in application code.

safe_sentences: The engine timing ran after the held-out run was scored, on tuning inputs only: 200 tuning seeds on one June commit graph (2,450 nodes, 7,077 edges), 200 file nodes of the frozen commit graph (5,464 nodes, 16,462 edges) and the 20 tuning questions. No held-out task or question was timed.

The three engines took turns in short blocks inside one container on six pinned CPUs, one engine at a time (no two blocks overlapped in time), over five passes from 08:05 to 11:21 UTC on 2026-11-13; every engine was first in about a third of the rounds.

The PC was busy throughout: other work used a median of about 6 of its 24 logical CPUs during the blocks. 148 of the 2,148 block attempts in the passes were repeated because other work exceeded 12 CPUs, and 6 blocks were kept and flagged after three repeats; dropping them changes nothing.
All three engines returned the same ranked answer for every seed, in every pass, at every thread setting, warm and cold, and the same answers to the 20 questions.
An independent recomputation from the raw block files reproduced every number in the engine table and all 180 engine-to-engine verdicts.

For the selected configuration (the frozen primary), SQLite answered fastest: median 14.5 ms per ranking on the tuning graph and 32.7 ms on the frozen graph, against 41.5 and 71.2 ms for LadybugDB and 70.3 and 98.7 ms for DuckDB with DuckPGQ (one thread, warm). These differences hold in wall and CPU time in all five passes.

Between LadybugDB and DuckDB-with-DuckPGQ no difference is stated for the frozen primary warm median (71.2 against 98.7 ms): LadybugDB was lower in all five passes, but the 27.5 ms gap is smaller than the 36 ms spread between DuckDB's passes, so under the declared rule it stays inside the noise.

For the PageRank configurations (S1 and the 2-hop base), the arm that runs PageRank in JavaScript over a cached adjacency (LadybugDB) was fastest, and the arm that runs it as about 270 SQL statements per ranking (SQLite) was slowest: frozen graph S1 17 ms, 58 ms and 256 ms (LadybugDB, DuckDB, SQLite). With the application caches dropped, LadybugDB is 51 ms and still lowest. This compares PageRank implementations, not graph operators.
For the 20 question lookups SQLite took about 0.3 ms per question, LadybugDB about 1.9 ms and DuckDB about 9 ms (warm median, frozen graph).

Building a store took about 0.35 to 0.9 s for SQLite, 0.6 to 0.7 s for DuckDB and 3.1 to 3.7 s for LadybugDB (median over five builds), and a one-file update 0.18 to 0.27 s for SQLite and DuckDB (no difference between them beyond the noise) against 0.52 to 0.63 s for LadybugDB; the stores hold different extra tables, so this compares the three designs, not the engines alone.
Every per-query time is a few milliseconds to a few hundred milliseconds on graphs of a few thousand nodes; the test does not show whether these differences matter for an agent working in a session.
must_not_claim: Graph engines are faster than SQL (or than SQLite) at answering "what is connected to this code?".
SQLite is faster (or slower) than the graph engines in general; the order depends on the configuration and on where each arm runs its ranking.
LadybugDB computes PageRank, or the primary ranking, faster in its graph engine: both run in JavaScript in the LadybugDB arm.
The S1 and 2-hop base timings show a graph operator against SQL: they compare a JavaScript PageRank over an application cache, one recursive SQL statement and about 270 SQL statements per ranking.
DuckPGQ's graph operators are slower than SQL: most of its timed work is SQL, and the primary reach uses its iterativelength() function.

LadybugDB starts (cold) faster than DuckDB or SQLite: its cold figure leaves out a facts load of about 90 to 180 ms that only LadybugDB needs; counted in, it is slower than SQLite on every class except frozen S1 and base, and slower than DuckDB on the frozen graph.
149 differences between the engines hold (as a count of separate findings): 45 of them repeat a 1-thread statement under the "best threads" label.
The timing was taken on a quiet machine.
A "best thread setting" is faster than one thread (it is a calibration pick; for LadybugDB frozen primary and SQLite questions it is not faster beyond the noise).
LadybugDB needs less query code than SQL (2 statements and 471 characters): its algorithm code is in JavaScript and is not counted in the query-text measure.
Store build time, update time or size on disk measure the engines alone: each arm stores different extra tables.
Any engine is better for this project, or should be adopted, on the strength of these timings.
An agent finishes tasks faster with any of these stores.
Anything timed here was measured on held-out tasks or questions.
The timings hold for larger graphs, other repositories or other machines.

rows.measured: Partly: the storage engine, on the same parser facts. The same facts in SQLite (relational), LadybugDB (graph) and the DuckDB graph layer gave the same answers. Store size, build, one-file update and query times were measured by the timing run.
rows.not: Answers cannot differ in size when they are identical. The store sizes compare three designs that keep different extra tables, not the engines alone.
rows.wider: The engine is not re-tested; whether a graph of model-read meaning helps is a separate, untested question (row "store the semantic relations").

rows.measured: Read as graph neighbourhood: how far the walk goes (1 to 6 hops, and unbounded) moved tuning recall more than anything else. Read as place in the code: the same-folder floor.
rows.not: Read as closeness in an embedding space: no embedding arm was run, because it needs a model download.
rows.wider: The design check asks for each reading to be declared in advance: neighbourhood and impact queries in A1, the same-folder floor, and embedding arm E only if you allow the download.

rows.measured: Nothing about time. Each commit had its own snapshot of facts (190 snapshots), used only as a build cache.
rows.not: Facts with validity periods, "as of commit K" queries, and a temporal knowledge graph as shipped (for example Graphiti).
rows.wider: A3t: validity by commit ancestry, split from cached conclusions as the design check asks (P1). Graphiti (arm T) only if you choose it; the draft does not recommend it now.

rows.words: caching concepts and invalidation ... wouldnt cache databases help with this??
rows.measured: No cache was tested. The facts cost no model tokens and rebuild in about 5.3 s per commit, so there was nothing expensive to cache.
rows.not: Conclusions that carry the facts they rest on and are invalidated when one of them changes; stale answers served.
rows.wider: K0: replay the 190 snapshots under five cache policies, with no model and no tokens. K1 and A3c with an agent only if K0 passes; A3s is the same store with invalidation switched off. Your prompt cache already serves 94.9 % of FixFlow context tokens as cache reads. Those are still tokens the model processes: the prompt cache lowers price and delay, not the token count (protocol-v2.md). A database cache that keeps unneeded content out of the window would therefore cut cached and uncached tokens alike; how much is untested. The token report also measured that only 0.5 to 1.5 % of a window is content fetched a second time inside the same window, so a cache that only stops repeat reads within one session would save little; stopping a first, unneeded read is the untested part.

rows.words: using caching on top of it so we dont traverse unnecessary nodes
rows.measured: Traversal time in three engines, cold and warm: milliseconds per ranking.
rows.not: A cache over traversals. It cannot move the token bill: a traversal costs milliseconds, one model step about 6.6 s, and the bill is counted in tokens.
rows.wider: Not a token lever, so not re-tested.

rows.not: Meaning that a model reads from documents: rules, reasons, decisions and document-to-code links. This is the layer graphify adds.

graphify.lacks: No time validity, no history and no stored summaries; invalidation is per file by content hash. Queries are lexical seed-finding followed by breadth-first expansion, cut at 2,000 tokens by default. The tested graph has changed-together history, route-to-call and table read/write edges that graphify lacks (its changed-together analysis is an open pull request, #4544).

headline.corpus: 29 Python files from three public repositories, 14 documentation files, 5 research-paper PDFs and 4 images
headline.how: Corpus tokens estimated as words times 4/3; answer tokens as characters divided by 4; the average over 5 generic questions. No answer was graded. Measured once by the maintainer, on 2026-04-04, and not re-run after the counting change shipped in version 0.9.87 (pull request 4348).
headline.reading: It compares reading the whole corpus with one capped graph answer, so any retrieval method would score high. Keeping only the 29 code files (dropping the 5 PDFs, 14 documentation files and 4 images) takes it from 71.5x to 8.8x.

measurements.title: Graphify's own code-agent result (ERPNext)
measurements.text: Key-fact coverage 82.0 % with the graph tool against 70.8 % for grep and read, with one agent model. No interval; one question flipping moves the score by a similar amount; the harness is not public.

measurements.title: graphify-bench: the 940-run agent benchmark
measurements.n: 940 runs, one repetition per task, one synthetic corpus (477 code files, 139 design documents)
measurements.text: Real headless coding-agent runs; the graphify arm is exactly what its installer produces. Intervals resample tasks only, so run-to-run noise is unmeasured. The usage counter covers only the main session, so subagent tokens are missed; the graphify arms carry skill text and nudges and never spawn subagents, while the baseline delegated to subagents in about half its runs.
measurements.extra: Against a baseline with subagents disabled, code tasks on the strong model cost +107k tokens [+38k, +180k] with graphify. Contradiction hunt: 4 tasks, graphify found 4 of 4 against 2 of 4 (F1 0.94 against 0.68), on 12 contradictions the benchmark's author planted. On doc-and-code questions the strong model's cost fell by 0.084 US dollars [-0.180, -0.005].
measurements.downgrade: The refuter downgrades the doc-and-code positive to weak and directional: 80 % against 70 % on 20 tasks is a difference of 2 tasks with no accuracy interval, the token interval crosses zero, the weaker model reverses the sign (75 % against 80 %), and the arms differ by more than the graph. The page itself states both 65 and 105 for the task count.

graphify.bottom_line: Graphify's headline compares one capped answer with reading everything. The controlled independent runs on code with a strong model found no accuracy gain and no clear token saving, which is in line with this test. The one positive sits in the document layer this test left out, and it is weak and directional.

wider.status: A design, not a result. Nothing in it has been built, run, installed or frozen; it is a draft for your decisions, with the corrections of the design check applied.
wider.question: On this repository, does a knowledge layer let an agent do the same work with fewer total tokens and no loss of correctness, and which layer earns its cost?
wider.outcome: Total tokens per task over all model calls, subagents included, plus the layer's build and update tokens spread over the tasks it served, plus its tool descriptions in every call; correctness against sealed references as a guard.

layers.label: Agent with ordinary search and read (the real baseline)
Structure: the tested code graph as one command-line tool
Meaning: model-read claims from product docs and commit messages

wider.controls: Controls beside them: A0p, a placebo tool with a description of equal length; A0x, a plain capped keyword index; A3s, the cached-conclusion store with invalidation switched off. Optional, your decision: E, an embedding entry point (a model download); T, Graphiti as shipped on set K only.

phases.title: Feasibility
phases.does: Do tests and type checkers run at old parents; how many change commits survive; how much needed-but-not-edited context each commit has; enough fresh commits?
phases.stop: STOP if fewer than 25 runnable commits, or the needed-but-not-edited column is near empty.
phases.fix: Design check P9: main has 0 product-code commits after the freeze, so the held-out set must be prospective: the first usable commits after the protocol is hashed, plus 14 days.

phases.title: Screens
phases.does: Break oracle by script; K0 cache replay over the 190 snapshots under five policies (none, whole repository, file hash, fact level, fact level with early cutoff); replay of the 139 recorded lookups.
phases.stop: STOP and fix if a fact-level policy serves any stale answer.
phases.fix: Design check P5: the draft stopped on any stale answer, but the file-hash policy is expected to serve some; its stale rate is a finding. The engine timing the check asked for here has now run (section H).

phases.title: Model layers
phases.does: Build the meaning layer (A2) and graphify's document layer (G2) twice on 10 parents.
phases.stop: STOP if build cost exceeds the agreed budget, or the two builds disagree on more than a quarter of anchored claims.
phases.fix: Design check P10: A3 needs the knowledge store built first, and your D1 audit and D1b yes come before any build.

phases.title: Pilot agent runs
phases.does: 12 change tasks with 4 arms and 3 runs each; 30 questions with 5 arms and 2 runs each. Then freeze sample size, thresholds and arms, and hash the protocol.
phases.stop: STOP if adoption is below 20 % in every tool arm without steering, or the leak audit finds leaks.
phases.fix: Design check P2 and P3: as drafted, only savings of 20 % or more are detected reliably, and the correctness guard passes a harmless arm only 51 to 64 % of the time; choose the margins before the pilot ends.

phases.title: Held-out main run, once
phases.does: 40 change tasks with 4 arms and 3 runs; 70 questions with 6 arms and 2 runs; 80 break-oracle changes by script, then 30 with an agent.
phases.stop: Verdicts only by the rules fixed in advance.
phases.fix: Design check P4: the stale-answer bound needs about 150 cache hits, so it is computed on set K (600 claim-steps), not on change tasks.

phases.title: Score and report
phases.does: Score by script where the answer is a set or a test result; a judge only for rubric questions; three refuters; the must-not-claim lists bind the report.
phases.fix: Design check P13: results speak to product-code tasks only; no verdict is possible on design and document work, where most measured spend is.

cost.why: In this harness an agent call averages 113k to 123k tokens of context, about 60k of it fixed prefix, so the draft's per-run figure is likely 2 to 4 times too low. All recorded FixFlow context tokens so far are 2.13 billion.

wider.verdict_note: Graph type (graph, knowledge graph, temporal knowledge graph) gets descriptive step contrasts with intervals; only A1, A3 and G2 against A0 can carry a verdict, unless you make the step contrasts primary (design check P1). A "cannot tell" does not mean a layer does not help.
